I’d start by treating the capacity increase as one data point, not the explanation. First I’d compare queue depth, consumer throughput, processing latency, and error rates before and after the change, then review worker logs, traces, and any deployment or config changes around the time the spikes began. That helps me see whether the backlog is tied to a specific workload pattern, a downstream dependency, or something like retries, timeouts, or lock contention.

Next I’d form a few tests to narrow it down. For example, I’d check whether the delay follows particular message types, partitions, tenants, or time windows, and whether the slowdown appears only when a downstream service or database is under pressure. I’d also look at whether the added workers are actually getting useful work, or if they’re being blocked, failing and retrying, or competing on a shared resource. If possible, I’d compare one worker group or queue shard against another to see whether the problem is isolated.

Then I’d interpret the pattern rather than just the raw metrics. If queue depth rises when retries or external latency spike, that points to a dependency problem rather than insufficient capacity. If worker CPU is low but wait time is high, that suggests blocking or backpressure, not raw compute shortage. I’d use those observations to decide the next fix, and only keep scaling if the evidence shows the bottleneck is still pure throughput.

I wouldn’t assume the worker increase fixed the right thing. I’d go back and look at the queue metrics, worker logs, traces, and any config or rollout changes around when the delay started. Then I’d compare what changed before and after the capacity tweak so I can see whether the backlog lines up with retries, downstream slowness, or some specific class of messages.

After that I’d test a couple of hypotheses instead of guessing. For example, I’d check whether the spikes happen for one queue shard, one payload type, or when a dependent service gets slow. I’d also want to know whether workers are busy processing, stuck waiting on I/O, or failing and requeuing jobs. If I can isolate the pattern, that tells me whether the issue is capacity, contention, or something outside the worker pool.

The main thing is to use the observations to rule causes in or out. If the delay tracks downstream latency or retry storms, then more workers just amplify the pressure. If the workers are idle but the queue is still growing, that points somewhere else in the pipeline.

I’d inspect queue metrics, worker logs, traces, and recent config or deploy changes around the spike. Then I’d test whether the backlog follows a specific message type, shard, or downstream dependency, and whether workers are blocked, retrying, or actually processing steadily. From that pattern I can tell if the problem is capacity, contention, or an external bottleneck, instead of assuming the first change was the right fix.

I’d begin by reviewing the queue depth, worker throughput, and recent deployment history so I can see what changed around the time the delay started. I’d also check logs and traces for obvious errors, timeouts, or retry behavior, because those can explain why work is still building up even after more workers were added.

From there I’d look for patterns in when the spikes happen, such as whether they line up with certain message types, particular time windows, or external service slowdowns. If the backlog is still increasing, I’d compare the current worker behavior with the earlier baseline to see whether the added capacity is being used effectively or whether the work is getting delayed somewhere else in the pipeline.

I’d use that information to narrow down the likely cause before making another change.

I’d first go back to the queue stats, worker logs, traces, and any recent deploy or config changes. I’d want to see what was happening when the spikes show up and whether there are errors, retries, or timeouts that explain why the backlog is still growing.

Then I’d look for any pattern in the delay, like whether it’s tied to certain jobs, certain times of day, or an upstream service getting slow. I’d compare that against the worker behavior so I can tell whether the extra capacity is being used or whether the slowdown is happening somewhere else. That should narrow the list of causes before I try another fix.

I’d check queue depth, worker logs, traces, and recent deploy/config changes, then look for patterns in the spikes and any retries or timeouts. I’d compare current behavior to the earlier baseline to narrow down whether the issue is in the workers or somewhere upstream before changing anything else.

I’d probably focus on the worker pool first, since the initial fix didn’t clear the delay. I’d keep increasing capacity until the queue starts dropping, because if work is still accumulating that usually means the system just needs more throughput. I might skim the logs, but I wouldn’t spend too much time there unless there’s a clear error, since intermittent spikes are often just load variation.

If the backlog still doesn’t move, I’d assume the queue implementation or the workers themselves are the problem and tune them further. At that point I’d look at scaling settings and maybe increase concurrency again, because the most direct path is usually to add more processing power until the delay goes away.

I’d mostly keep pushing on capacity. If the first increase didn’t fix it, I’d add more workers and see if the queue catches up, since the backlog is probably just outpacing the current setup. I’d only dig into logs or traces if the extra scaling still doesn’t help, because those can take a while to sort through.

My assumption would be that the system is just under-provisioned for the spike pattern, so I’d adjust the worker count and concurrency first and use that to get the queue under control.

I’d keep scaling the workers and concurrency until the queue clears, and only check logs or traces if that still doesn’t work. My first assumption would be that the backlog is mainly a throughput problem, so I’d push capacity higher before spending much time investigating other causes.
